title: KVCache staleness & prefetch tuning - Meridian Therapeutics deep dive
summary: Deep technical session about KV cache staleness, prefetch heuristics, NUMA/oom behaviors on private deployments, and telemetry-driven eviction policies. Agreed next steps: run targeted prefetch experiment, share KV telemetry dashboard, schedule on-prem NUMA tuning session.
next_steps: Redwood to share KV telemetry dashboard link and suggested prefetch configs by 2025-04-25
Meridian to run 48h prefetch experiment on staging and report token-level latency by 2025-05-02
Schedule on-prem NUMA and disk-backed spillback session w/ Meridian SREs (target week of 2025-05-05)
SE to provide sample workload profiling script and token distribution histogram
action_items: Omar Rizvi: export KV hit/miss heatmap and upload to shared drive by 2025-04-24
Marco Diaz: enable detailed KV logging on staging for 48h and share logs 2025-05-02
Jasleen Singh: prepare prefetch config template and recommended thresholds by 2025-04-25
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-21 16:00 UTC | Duration: 62m | Attendees: Lena Park, Omar Rizvi, Jasleen Singh (Redwood) — Dr. Priya Nair, Marco Diaz, Dana Holt, Evan Wu (Meridian)

[00:00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick goal for the call — deep dive into KV cache staleness and prefetch tuning on your private deployment, and whether our predictive prefetching helps your long-context use cases.

[00:00:15] Dr. Priya Nair: Thanks Lena. We're seeing tail latency regressions when sessions go past 8k tokens, plus some weird spike in memory usage that looks like repeated cache evictions. We ran a basic LRU and saw thrashing.

[00:00:34] Omar Rizvi: Got it. Can you describe your workload distribution? Are prefixes highly overlapping across requests or pretty unique?

[00:00:45] Marco Diaz: It's mixed. A lot of reuse for the same patient record prompts — so prefix reuse is pretty high for some routes, but we also spin up analytic jobs that feed in large synthetic contexts. The spikes come when the analytic jobs kick off.

[00:01:05] Jasleen Singh: That pattern plays right into our prefetch heuristics — high prefix reuse benefits from proactive prefetch, but diversity-heavy jobs can cause footprint explosion unless we tune eviction windows.

[00:01:18] Dana Holt: Quick question — on-prem we've got NUMA nodes, and the processes are pinned. Could that cause uneven eviction or paging behavior?

[00:01:28] Omar Rizvi: Absolutely. On-prem NUMA and memory fragmentation change the latency curve. If the KV store is memory-mapped (mmap) and pages are remote to the CPU doing the decode, you'll see tail latencies and stalls that look like evictions but are actually NUMA locality issues.

[00:01:45] Dr. Priya Nair: We are using a memory-mapped KV layer in our private bundle to avoid copy overheads. We suspected something like that.

[00:01:53] Lena Park: Important to separate two things we saw: 1) true eviction where the key is removed from the in-memory index and requires rehydration from spill-to-disk, and 2) staleness/locality where the key is present but page fault or cross-node access causes a pause. Both look like "misses" at different layers.

[00:02:12] Evan Wu: Can Redwood's telemetry distinguish between an L1 miss, an L2 miss, and a page fault?

[00:02:18] Omar Rizvi: We instrument token-level fetches. We can tag events as cache-index-miss (no pointer), cache-value-miss (value not resident), and page-fault (OS-level). The challenge is that standard logs often conflate them because of time granularity. We'll share a more fine-grained trace that breaks down the latency histogram by fetch outcome.

[00:02:38] Marco Diaz: That would be super helpful. Right now our graphs show an uptick in "cache miss" latency but not the root cause.

[00:02:45] Jasleen Singh: For eviction policies — you said you ran LRU. Did you try a frequency-aware policy or a windowed-LRU that decays items older than X minutes?

[00:02:58] Marco Diaz: We tried plain LRU and a naive LFU sketch, but LFU kept promoting stale analytic prefixes that only ran once a day and bumped out hot patient prefixes. So LFU was worse for us.

[00:03:12] Omar Rizvi: That's a classic issue: LFU without decay can cause cold-but-frequently-once events to pollute the top. We recommend a hybrid: time-decayed LFU or an Adaptive Replacement Cache (ARC) that keeps a balance between recency and frequency. It tends to handle bursty analytics plus sustained reuse.

[00:03:32] Dana Holt: Can Redwood run ARC in the runtime today? Does it add CPU overhead?

[00:03:38] Jasleen Singh: We have a user-space ARC implementation that we've tested on CPU and GPU hosts; CPU overhead is tiny relative to the cost of a token decode. The memory overhead is modest: a few bytes per key for counters and timestamps. On small key sizes it adds up but is manageable.

[00:03:54] Dr. Priya Nair: About prefetching — we worried that aggressive prefetch would saturate GPU memory and evict already-cached KV entries. How does Redwood prevent prefetch from causing self-inflicted thrash?

[00:04:06] Omar Rizvi: Two mechanisms: prefetch budget and adaptive prefetch backpressure. Budget is a hard cap on total prefetch bytes per model worker. Backpressure uses observed miss/hit rates and decoder latency to scale down prefetch frequency. Additionally, prefetch can be constrained to only pre-warm prefixes with >threshold reuse probability.

[00:04:26] Evan Wu: How do you estimate reuse probability? Do you rely on a simple moving average of hit counts or a learned model?

[00:04:33] Jasleen Singh: We currently use a hybrid heuristic: exponential moving average of prefix hit rate plus contextual signals (route ID, user cohort). For customers with enough data we can plug in a lightweight classifier to predict reuse — but that requires training and privacy constraints.

[00:04:50] Marco Diaz: Privacy is important — especially for patient-related routes. We'd prefer no ML model that uses PII. Is the heuristic robust enough?

[00:04:58] Lena Park: Yes; heuristics get you 80% of gains. The classifier is optional and we support only aggregate, non-PII signals if used.

[00:05:07] Dana Holt: Another angle — spill-to-disk format. Right now our spill files are compressed, which saves space but comes with decompression CPU overhead when rehydrating hot keys. Is there a middle ground?

[00:05:18] Omar Rizvi: Right — compressing spill reduces IO but increases CPU at rehydrate time. Options: LZ4 inline for fast decompress, or chunk-level compression where frequently-accessed items are kept uncompressed. We can also use a two-tier spill: small hot-chunks uncompressed, cold archive compressed. That helps reduce rehydrate latency for hot items.

[00:05:38] Evan Wu: On staging we saw rehydrate taking 30-60ms for compressed chunks which kills conversational latency.

[00:05:44] Jasleen Singh: That's too high for chat. Aim for uncompressed or LZ4 with prefetch for conversational routes. For analytics jobs, compression is fine.

[00:05:54] Dr. Priya Nair: You mentioned prefetch-trigger heuristics. Could you outline a sample config we could try?

[00:06:02] Jasleen Singh: Sure — sample prefetch config we recommend:
- prefetch_enabled: true
- prefetch_budget_mb: 512 per worker (tunable)
- prefetch_threshold_rate: 0.2 (probability a prefix is reused)
- prefetch_backoff_ms: 50 (minimum spacing between prefetches to avoid bursts)
- prefetch_priority: route_scoped, only routes in whitelist for chat
- decay_window_minutes: 30 (decay counters older than this)

[00:06:28] Marco Diaz: 512MB per worker might be high for our smaller GPU instances. Recommend starting lower.

[00:06:33] Omar Rizvi: Yes start with 64-128MB in staging and monitor miss curves. Also enable the telemetry tag 'prefetch:initiated' so we can correlate prefetches with hit uplift.

[00:06:45] Dana Holt: About telemetry — we need token-level histograms and also per-prefix TTL and last-accessed timestamps. Is that available out-of-the-box?

[00:06:54] Jasleen Singh: We'll provide a KV telemetry schema that includes: prefix_id, last_access_ts, hit_count_ema, miss_count, last_prefetch_ts, resident_bytes, spill_status. We'll push a Grafana dashboard template.

[00:07:08] Dr. Priya Nair: Great. One more on quantization — we recently moved to 4-bit quant for weights to save memory. Does that change KV footprint or access patterns?

[00:07:18] Omar Rizvi: Quantization primarily affects model weights memory, not KV key-value store per se. But lower precision can change tokenization behavior and sequence length packing which indirectly changes KV access density (more aggressive packing -> more tokens per batch -> different hit distributions). Also, some quant libraries change memory alignment which can affect page residency. Worth validating end-to-end.

[00:07:40] Evan Wu: We also have a few dedicated instances in your Dedicated offering; would moving some analytic jobs to those reduce pressure on the hosted worker pools?

[00:07:48] Lena Park: Yes separating analytical workloads to dedicated nodes with larger batch windows is a recommended pattern. Analytical workloads tolerate higher latency and can be batched, reducing contention on chat-focused pools.

[00:07:59] Marco Diaz: For the prefetch experiment, can we run a canary where 10% of chat traffic has prefetch on and compare tail latency and cost per token over 48 hours?

[00:08:08] Jasleen Singh: Absolutely — we can provide the canary config and traffic-splitting instructions. We suggest metrics to compare: p95/p99 tail latency, KV hit ratio, rehydrate count, average GPU memory usage, and additional cost due to prefetch.

[00:08:23] Dana Holt: Another nit — our SREs have seen time-of-day correlated evictions, like 03:00 jobs causing mass churn. Can prefetch be time-window aware?

[00:08:32] Omar Rizvi: Yes, prefetch policies can be windowed and rate-limited by cron schedules or calendar events. It's common to disable aggressive prefetch around heavy nightly jobs.

[00:08:42] Dr. Priya Nair: We care about auditability. If prefetch pulls in data from sensitive routes, will those measures be logged for compliance?

[00:08:50] Lena Park: Prefetch events are logged and can be tied to route IDs; we can filter PII at the telemetry layer. For Private deployments you control retention and export of those logs. We support KMS for encryption-at-rest for spill files.

[00:09:05] Evan Wu: About fallback behavior — if prefetch causes memory pressure, is there an automatic rollback to prefetch-off?

[00:09:13] Jasleen Singh: Yes, we have automatic fallback: if resident_bytes crosses a threshold or rehydrate latency increases beyond a SLO, prefetch ramps to zero and we revert to conservative eviction policy. That behavior is tunable.

[00:09:24] Marco Diaz: Let's talk observability — can Redwood annotate traces with whether a fetch was satisfied from in-memory vs spill vs page fault?

[00:09:31] Omar Rizvi: We can add a fetch_outcome tag to each token-level span: IN_MEMORY, SPILL_REHYDRATE, PAGE_FAULT. We'll include latency buckets and stack traces for the slowest events.

[00:09:42] Dana Holt: Perfect. For the action plan: we'll enable detailed KV logging on staging for 48 hours, run a 10% prefetch canary, and share results. Redwood will provide dashboard and config templates.

[00:09:54] Lena Park: Quick recap — primary hypothesis: your tail latencies are a mix of NUMA/page locality and eviction triggered by analytics spike. Experiments: 1) enable detailed telemetry to separate page-faults from misses; 2) run canary prefetch at low budget; 3) try ARC or decayed-LFU instead of naive LFU; 4) adjust spill strategy (uncompressed hot-chunks).

[00:10:13] Dr. Priya Nair: Sounds good. Who owns the telemetry export?

[00:10:18] Marco Diaz: I will enable logs and drop them in the shared S3 bucket, that's Marco.

[00:10:23] Lena Park: Action items already captured — Omar will upload the KV heatmap and Grafana template; Jasleen will share prefetch config; Marco will run the 48h staging logs. We'll reconvene after the staging run.

[00:10:36] Evan Wu: One last quick question — any recommended default backoff curve for prefetch to avoid thundering herd if multiple workers prefetch same prefix?

[00:10:44] Omar Rizvi: Use jittered exponential backoff with a small global dedupe: a single worker can claim a prefetch token for prefix X for T ms to prevent duplication. Backoff parameters: base 20ms, max 500ms, jitter 20%.

[00:10:58] Dr. Priya Nair: Thanks, team.

[00:11:02] Lena Park: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts.

[00:11:06] Meeting end.

Notes: transcript has some automatic transcription errors (names and acronyms), speakers sometimes overlap. Logs referenced: /shared/meridian/kvcache/staging-2025-04-21.tar.gz, KV telemetry dashboard link (to be provided by Redwood).
